title: Here Is My Servant: Justice for the Nations
summary: God presents his Servant, chosen and filled with his Spirit, who will bring justice to the nations quietly and gently, not breaking a bruised reed, and who is appointed as a covenant for the people and a light to the nations. The whole earth is called to sing a new song as the LORD goes out like a warrior to lead the blind home. The chapter ends by turning to Israel, the servant who is blind and deaf, and explaining that the exile was God's own judgment on a people who would not listen.
story: In chapter 41 God called Israel “My servant” and promised to help them. Chapter 42 opens with “Here is My Servant,” but the figure described here does something Israel has not done: he brings justice to the nations with patience and faithfulness. Then, at the end of the chapter, the word “servant” is applied to Israel again, this time to a servant who is blind and deaf. The chapter sets these two portraits side by side, and the tension between them drives the chapters that follow. God's purpose for his servant is clear; the question is who will fulfill it.
historical:
The setting remains the late period of the Babylonian exile, before Cyrus's capture of Babylon in 539 BC, whether these words were first spoken then or foreseen earlier (see the note on chapter 40). The final section (verses 22 to 25) describes the exiles' condition plainly: a people plundered and imprisoned, with no one to demand their release. The prophet insists that this was not the triumph of Babylon's gods but the LORD's own judgment, a claim that made the exile interpretable and therefore survivable.

The places named in verse 11 widen the horizon. Kedar was a people of the Arabian desert, known in the Old Testament for their tents and flocks, and Sela is probably a site in the rugged country of Edom, southeast of Judah (the name means rock). Even these remote and often hostile peoples are called to sing.
cultural:
The images of verse 3 come from ordinary life. A reed was the flimsiest plant of the riverbank, used for pens or measuring rods, and a bruised one was good only for throwing away. A lamp's wick, made of flax, smoldered and smoked when the oil ran low, and the natural reaction was to snuff it out. The Servant does neither. In a world where rulers proved their strength by crushing the weak, and where royal proclamations were shouted in the streets, this Servant brings justice without shouting and without breaking what is already damaged.

The phrase “to bring prisoners out of the dungeon” in verse 7 drew on a real feature of ancient life: debtors, captives, and political prisoners were often kept in dark pits or cisterns. A new king sometimes marked his accession by releasing prisoners, and the chapter uses that practice as a picture of what the Servant does.
literary: Verses 1 to 4 are the first of four passages that the German scholar Bernhard Duhm, in 1892, labeled the Servant Songs (the others are 49:1-6, 50:4-9, and 52:13 to 53:12). Many scholars extend this first song through verse 9, since verses 5 to 9 address the same figure. The song is framed by the word “justice,” which appears three times in four verses, and it describes the Servant almost entirely by what he will not do: cry out, break, extinguish, grow weak. A hymn follows (verses 10 to 17), calling the whole earth to sing a new song, and it pictures God first as a warrior and then, startlingly, as a woman in labor who has been silent too long. The chapter closes with a disputation (verses 18 to 25) that turns the language of blindness on Israel, the servant who has eyes and does not see.

outline.t: The first Servant Song: justice brought gently to the nations
The Servant appointed as a covenant and a light
A new song for the LORD who goes out to lead the blind
Israel, the blind and deaf servant, and the reason for exile

doctrines.note: The Servant is chosen by God, filled with the Spirit, and sent to bring justice to the nations. The church has confessed from the beginning that this figure is fulfilled in Jesus, though the chapter itself leaves his identity open, as the hard question below explains.
“I will put My Spirit on Him.” In the Old Testament the Spirit of God equips particular people for a task. The Servant's gentle and unfailing work comes from that gift, not from force.
The Servant is “a light to the nations,” and the islands wait for his law. God's purpose was never Israel's restoration alone; it was the blessing of the nations, as promised to Abraham.
The exile is explained as the LORD's own act: “Was it not the LORD, against whom we have sinned?” The same God who judged is the one who will restore.

words.note: Mishpat, justice. The word covers a court's verdict, the right order of a society, and the just ways God requires. The Servant's mission is to establish mishpat among the nations, which includes but goes beyond law courts: it is the setting right of what is wrong.

Torah, instruction or law. The islands wait for the Servant's torah (verse 4), and God magnifies his torah (verse 21), which Israel would not obey (verse 24). The word means teaching and direction, not merely a code of rules.

Berit, covenant, a binding relationship with promises and obligations. Remarkably, the Servant is not said to make a covenant but to be one: “a covenant for the people.” His person embodies God's bond with his people.

Iwwer, blind. The word appears six times, first for those whose eyes the Servant will open (verse 7), then for those God leads home (verse 16), and finally for Israel, God's servant, who sees and does not take it to heart (verse 19). Blindness names both Israel's plight and its fault.

christ: The New Testament applies this song directly to Jesus. Matthew 12:15-21 quotes Isaiah 42:1-4 at length to explain why Jesus healed the sick but told them not to make him known: he is the Servant who does not quarrel or cry out, and in whose name the nations will hope. At Jesus's baptism, the voice from heaven calls him the beloved Son in whom God is well pleased (Mark 1:11), words that many interpreters hear as combining Psalm 2 with Isaiah 42:1, while the Spirit descends on him as the Servant is promised the Spirit. Simeon's song in Luke 2:32 calls the infant Jesus a light for revelation to the Gentiles, echoing verse 6 (and 49:6). And Jesus's ministry of opening the eyes of the blind is presented in the Gospels as the fulfillment of what the Servant would do. The contrast within the chapter, between the faithful Servant and blind Israel, is part of how the New Testament understands Jesus as the true Israel who does what the nation could not.

hard.q: Who is the Servant in this song?
hard.a:
The chapter itself never names him, and readers have given four main answers. Many Jewish interpreters, and many modern scholars, identify the Servant with Israel, pointing to 41:8-9 and 49:3, where Israel is explicitly called God's servant; the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, even adds the names Jacob and Israel to verse 1. Others see the prophet himself, commissioned to speak to the nations. Others identify a particular historical individual: suggestions have included Cyrus, who is also said to be called and upheld by God, and figures such as Moses or a king of David's line. Still others read the Servant as the coming Messiah; the Aramaic paraphrase of Isaiah known as the Targum reads verse 1 that way.

Many interpreters, Christian and Jewish, combine these views. The Servant is Israel in its calling, but Israel as it is proves blind and deaf (verses 18 to 25), so the calling narrows to a faithful individual who embodies Israel and fulfills its mission, including a mission to Israel itself (49:5-6). Christians confess that Jesus is that Servant, while recognizing that the song's first readers would have seen the figure only in outline.

questions: The Servant will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a smoldering wick. Who in your life is a bruised reed, and what would gentleness toward them look like?
God describes himself in this chapter both as a warrior and as a woman in labor. What does each image show about his commitment to his people?
Israel had eyes and did not see, ears and did not hear. Where might you be seeing much without paying attention?
